title: Alibaba Sells Gaming Unit Lingxi Games for Over $2 Billion in AI Pivot
excerpt: Chinese tech giant reaches agreement with private equity firm Trustar Capital to offload its gaming business as it doubles down on AI and cloud infrastructure.
body:
• Alibaba has agreed to sell its gaming unit Lingxi Games to Trustar Capital (formerly CITIC Capital) for more than $2 billion.
  • The deal marks Alibaba's latest non-core asset divestiture as it redirects capital toward AI and cloud computing.
  • Lingxi Games, known for "Three Kingdoms: Strategy Edition," will retain its current management under CEO Zhou Bingshu.
  • The sale concludes a months-long process during which Alibaba approached at least five potential buyers.

Alibaba Group is selling its gaming subsidiary Lingxi Games to Asia-focused private equity firm Trustar Capital in a deal valued at more than $2 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter and an internal memo reviewed by Reuters. The transaction represents one of the largest gaming business divestitures by a major Chinese internet company in recent years.

The Deal

Under the agreement, Alibaba will transfer its entire stake in Lingxi to Trustar, formerly known as CITIC Capital. CEO Zhou Bingshu informed staff of the deal in an internal memo on Monday, stating that he and Lingxi's management team would continue to lead the company after the ownership change. Bloomberg News, which first reported the memo, cited sources valuing the deal at a minimum of $1.5 billion.

The memo did not disclose the precise value or expected closing date, nor did it detail regulatory approvals or conditions attached to the transaction. Neither Lingxi, Alibaba, nor Trustar immediately responded to requests for comment.

Strategic Retrenchment

The sale is the latest in a series of non-core asset divestitures by Alibaba as it sharpens its focus on artificial intelligence and cloud infrastructure. The company has committed to investing 380 billion yuan (approximately $56 billion) over three years in AI and cloud, while its core e-commerce and instant retail businesses demand sustained heavy investment.

"Alibaba has been reviewing non-core assets as it directs capital and management attention toward strategic priorities including AI and cloud."

— Reuters

Alibaba had been seeking a buyer for Lingxi for some time. Earlier reports indicated the company had approached at least five potential acquirers, including publicly listed gaming companies 37 Interactive Entertainment, China Ruyi, Century Huatong, and Giant Network, as well as two private equity firms. Initial valuations ranged from 7 to 9 billion yuan ($1 to $1.3 billion), but the final agreement with Trustar exceeded those earlier figures.

Lingxi Games in Transition

Guangzhou-based Lingxi Games is best known for "Three Kingdoms: Strategy Edition," a multiplayer strategy title developed in collaboration with Japan's Koei Tecmo Holdings. The company has approximately 1,200 employees across five in-house development studios.

The sale extends a period of change for Lingxi. A planned external fundraising process stalled in late 2023 after China proposed tighter regulations for the online gaming sector. The company also underwent a management reshuffle in 2024, with Zhou taking the CEO role after founder Zhan Zhonghui departed.

Market Impact

Alibaba's Hong Kong-listed shares edged higher on Monday following the news. The stock has traded between $92 and $193 over the past year. Investors have generally welcomed the company's strategy of shedding non-core businesses to fund its AI ambitions, with Alibaba's Qwen AI model emerging as a key competitive asset against domestic rivals Baidu and ByteDance.

It remains unclear whether Alibaba will retain any commercial ties with Lingxi after the sale, including publishing partnerships, cloud services, or technology agreements.
